FINDING_ID: IM_F017
SEVERITY: 0.82
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.75
DESCRIPTION: `_verify_remediation_outcomes` escalation path creates a zombie remediation entry that can never be verified or cleared. When a remediation is INEFFECTIVE, the code increments `state["chain_idx"]` and resets `state["applied_round"]` and `state["metric_at_apply"]` — but it does NOT check whether the new `chain_idx` exceeds the length of the remediation chain. The entry persists in `self._remediation_state` indefinitely. On subsequent rounds, `_verify_remediation_outcomes` will keep re-evaluating this entry, find the metric hasn't improved (because no actual transform was applied — the chain is exhausted), and emit another INEFFECTIVE diagnosis with an ever-incrementing `chain_idx`. The only code that removes entries is the `improved=True` branch (`del self._remediation_state[pathology_key]`). The caller `apply_diagnosis()` calls `record_chain_exhaustion()` when the chain is exhausted, but `_verify_remediation_outcomes` has no awareness of chain length — it operates purely on the `_remediation_state` dict. This produces an infinite escalation loop of spurious INEFFECTIVE diagnoses, each recommending a chain step that doesn't exist.
PROPOSED_FIX: In the INEFFECTIVE branch of `_verify_remediation_outcomes`, look up the chain length from `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS` (once defined). If `state["chain_idx"] + 1 >= len(chain)`, call `self.record_chain_exhaustion(pathology_key)`, delete the entry from `self._remediation_state`, and emit a CRITICAL diagnosis instead of the escalation message. Alternatively, add a `max_chain_idx` field to the remediation state at `set_remediation_state` time.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F018
SEVERITY: 0.78
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.70
DESCRIPTION: `record_model_round` consecutive failure counter (`_model_failure_counts`) resets to 0 on ANY non-failed round, but `record_round` Check 1 (kappa stuck) uses `_pathology_counts` which only resets when the pathology resolves. This creates an asymmetry: a model that fails rounds [0,1], succeeds round 2, then fails rounds [3,4] will have `consecutive=2` at round 4 and trigger the diagnosis — but the `_pathology_counts[f"model_failure_{model_id}"]` was never reset at round 2 because the reset logic is inside the `else` branch of the consecutive check (which only fires when `consecutive < 2`). The `persistence` counter monotonically increases across non-consecutive failure bursts, inflating severity to CRITICAL prematurely. A model with two separate single-failure events (rounds 0 and 5) that each happen to coincide with another failure (rounds 1 and 6) will show `persistence=2` on the second burst and immediately escalate to CRITICAL, even though the model recovered fully between bursts.
PROPOSED_FIX: Reset `self._pathology_counts[key]` to 0 in the `else` (non-failed) branch of `record_model_round`, mirroring the pattern used in `record_round` for kappa/mu resolution. Add: `key = f"model_failure_{model_id}"; if self._pathology_counts.get(key, 0) > 0: self._resolved_counts[key] = self._resolved_counts.get(key, 0) + 1; self._pathology_counts[key] = 0`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F019
SEVERITY: 0.75
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.80
DESCRIPTION: `self_diagnose` Self-check 1 (low remediation success rate) and Self-check 2 (high false positive rate) can both fire in the same `record_round` call and apply contradictory adjustments. Self-check 1 widens detection windows (making detection less sensitive). Self-check 2 increases `_sensitivity_decay` (also making detection less sensitive, but through the adaptive window formula). Both adjustments compound: the effective window becomes `base * (higher_decay ^ resolved) * (1 + growth * persistent)` with a wider base AND faster decay. The extended P-pass for Self-check 1 does not know about the Self-check 2 adjustment that will be applied in the same call (it hasn't happened yet), so the cross-parameter contradiction check cannot catch this. The combined effect can make the immune layer nearly blind in a single round.
PROPOSED_FIX: Run all self-checks first to collect proposed adjustments, then run a single combined P-pass that evaluates all proposed changes together before applying any. This is the standard "collect-then-commit" pattern that prevents intra-round interaction blindness.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F020
SEVERITY: 0.72
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.65
DESCRIPTION: `check_dispatch_health` Pathology 4 (dispatch false positive) uses `key = f"dispatch_fp_{model_id}_{block_round}"` as a deduplication key in `_pathology_counts`, but this key is never checked by `effective_window` or any resolution logic. The `_pathology_counts[key] = 1` assignment prevents re-diagnosis of the same block event, but the key accumulates forever — one entry per (model, round) pair. More critically, the deduplication check `if key not in self._pathology_counts` means the diagnosis fires exactly once per block event, but the `pathology_key="dispatch_false_positive"` on the diagnosis is a generic key shared across all models. If `apply_diagnosis` routes remediation by `pathology_key`, a single remediation state entry for `"dispatch_false_positive"` will be overwritten by each new model's block event, losing the per-model remediation tracking.
PROPOSED_FIX: Use `pathology_key=f"dispatch_false_positive_{model_id}"` to maintain per-model remediation state. Alternatively, if the generic key is intentional (one remediation covers all dispatch FPs), document this and ensure `set_remediation_state` handles the multi-model case.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F021
SEVERITY: 0.70
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.55
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.detect_failure` UNDERPERFORM detection depends on `_performance_metric` which calls `_expected_performance` which calls `self.config.get_baseline(role)`. Per CC2_IM_F012 (VERIFIED: FALSE), this method may not exist. But even assuming it does exist and returns the correct `b_rho` vector, the performance metric `perf = (finding_count * mean_abstraction) / expected` is dimensionally incoherent. `expected = b_rho . q_m` is a dot product of weight coefficients and normalised fingerprint values — a dimensionless score in roughly [0, 1]. `actual = finding_count * mean_abstraction` is count × [0,1] — a value that scales with the number of findings (potentially 0–50+). The ratio `actual/expected` is therefore not a meaningful performance fraction; it's an unbounded positive number. The threshold `theta_under = 0.3` was presumably calibrated for a ratio where 1.0 = expected performance, but with `expected ≈ 0.3` (typical dot product) and `actual = 5 * 0.6 = 3.0`, the ratio is 10.0 — underperformance is nearly impossible to trigger. Conversely, a model producing 1 finding at abstraction 0.1 gives ratio ≈ 0.33, which barely exceeds the threshold despite genuinely poor output.
PROPOSED_FIX: Normalise the performance metric. Either: (a) define `expected` as the expected `finding_count * mean_abstraction` (not a fingerprint dot product), or (b) normalise `actual` to the same scale as `expected` by dividing by a calibration constant derived from historical round data.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F022
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.60
DESCRIPTION: `record_round` Check 2 (mu increasing) resolution logic resets `_pathology_counts["mu"]` to 0 when the mu-increasing condition is not met. But the mu-increasing condition requires `mu_increasing AND findings_not_increasing` — both must be true. If mu stops increasing but findings are also increasing, the `else` branch fires and marks mu as "resolved." This is incorrect: the pathology was "mu increasing while findings stable/declining." If findings start increasing too, the pathology didn't resolve — the situation changed to a different (non-pathological) state. The resolution should only fire when mu stabilises or decreases, regardless of finding trajectory. As written, a scenario where mu keeps increasing AND findings also increase will trigger resolution, even though the mu distortion may still be present (it's just masked by the finding increase).
PROPOSED_FIX: Split the resolution check: only resolve when `not mu_increasing` (mu has stabilised), regardless of the `findings_not_increasing` condition. The current compound `else` conflates "mu stopped increasing" with "findings started increasing" — only the former indicates the pathology resolved.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F023
SEVERITY: 0.65
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.70
DESCRIPTION: `_extended_p_pass_remediation` convergence check for "no new failures across iterations" compares failure signatures extracted via `f.split(" — ")[0]`, but the comparison logic is structurally broken beyond the string-splitting fragility noted in CC2_IM_F015. The code computes `prev_failures_for_sig = all_failures[:-len(iteration_failures)]` to get failures from all previous iterations. But `all_failures` is extended with `iteration_failures` at the end of each iteration BEFORE the convergence check runs. So on iteration 1, `all_failures` contains iteration 0's failures + iteration 1's failures. `all_failures[:-len(iteration_failures)]` correctly isolates iteration 0's failures. But on iteration 2, `all_failures` contains iterations 0+1+2. `all_failures[:-len(iteration_2_failures)]` gives iterations 0+1 combined — not just iteration 1. The "previous iteration" comparison is actually "all prior iterations combined," which means the convergence criterion is "no new failure types compared to the union of all prior iterations" rather than "no new failure types compared to the immediately preceding iteration." This is more conservative than intended and may prevent early convergence.
PROPOSED_FIX: Track per-iteration failure signature sets separately: `iteration_sigs: List[Set[str]] = []`. At each iteration, compute `current_sigs` and compare against `iteration_sigs[-1]` (the previous iteration only). Append `current_sigs` to `iteration_sigs` after the comparison.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F024
SEVERITY: 0.62
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.55
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.get_recovery` for `DOWNGRADE_ROLE` only handles `COL → PAR` downgrade. If the failing model's role is `PM` and the failure type is `UNDERPERFORM` (repeated), the code reaches the `UNDERPERFORM` branch and returns `DOWNGRADE_ROLE`. The subsequent role mutation checks `if current_role == Role.COL` and does nothing for PM. The PM retains its role, the `DOWNGRADE_ROLE` action is recorded in history, but no actual state change occurs. This is a silent no-op for PM underperformance — the system believes it took corrective action but didn't. Note: PM failures of type EMPTY/TIMEOUT/MALFORMED are handled by the PM-specific branch above, but UNDERPERFORM falls through to the standard policy table.
PROPOSED_FIX: Add PM handling to the DOWNGRADE_ROLE execution: if the model is PM, either (a) reassign PM role to the next-highest-scoring model and downgrade the current PM to PAR, or (b) return a different action (e.g., LOG_ONLY with a CRITICAL event) since PM downgrade has protocol implications. Document the design decision either way.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F025
SEVERITY: 0.58
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.45
DESCRIPTION: `record_model_round` parser_yield anomaly detection (response_chars > 2000 and finding_count == 0 and not failed) will never fire for models that timeout, because timeout is detected by `FailureHandler.detect_failure` which sets `failed=True` before `record_model_round` is called. But the more subtle issue is that the `not failed` guard means a model that produces a 5000-character response that is parseable but yields 0 findings due to format divergence will be diagnosed — but a model that produces a 5000-character response that is ALSO flagged as FORMAT failure (format_compliant=False) will have `failed=True` and skip this check entirely. The FORMAT failure path in `FailureHandler` returns `RETRY_CLARIFIED` or `DEGRADE`, neither of which addresses the root cause (parser incompatibility). The parser_yield diagnosis, which DOES identify the root cause, is suppressed by the very failure it should complement.
PROPOSED_FIX: Change the guard to `not failed or failure_type == FailureType.FORMAT` — allow parser_yield diagnosis to fire alongside FORMAT failures, since they share the same root cause (format divergence) but the parser_yield diagnosis provides more actionable information (re-extract with adaptive parser).
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F026
SEVERITY: 0.55
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.50
DESCRIPTION: `self_diagnose` Self-check 2 (high false positive rate) applies a standard P-pass (not extended), which is correct per the comment "Single-module (sensitivity_decay only)." However, the P-pass is implemented inline as a simple trend check (`fp_improving`), not by calling `_standard_p_pass_remediation`. This bypasses the three-check protocol (history, trend, regression risk) that the standard P-pass implements. Specifically, it skips Check 1 (has this exact adjustment failed before?) and Check 3 (known regression risk from step effectiveness). The inline check only looks at whether the FP rate is trending down in the last 2 self-diagnosis entries — a much weaker gate than the full standard P-pass. This inconsistency means Self-check 2 adjustments are less scrutinised than regular remediations.
PROPOSED_FIX: Route Self-check 2 through `_standard_p_pass_remediation` with `chain_key="high_false_positive_rate"`, `chain_idx=0`, `target_metric="false_positive_rate"` (would need to add FP rate to `_get_metric_history`). This ensures consistent P-pass rigour across all adjustment types.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F027
SEVERITY: 0.52
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.40
DESCRIPTION: `record_round` Check 5 (vocab saturation) uses a hardcoded window of 3 rounds (`if len(self._vocab_growth_history) >= 3` and `recent_vg = self._vocab_growth_history[-3:]`), but the config parameter `vocab_sustained_window` is set to 5. The config value is never referenced in this check. The comment says "require 5 consecutive rounds below threshold" but the code only checks 3. This means vocab saturation is diagnosed 2 rounds earlier than the config specifies, increasing false positive risk — exactly the problem the config parameter was introduced to prevent (per the comment about Exp14 recalibration and premature termination).
PROPOSED_FIX: Replace the hardcoded `3` with `self._config.vocab_sustained_window` (defaulting to 5 if config is None): `window = self._config.vocab_sustained_window if self._config else 5; if len(self._vocab_growth_history) >= window: recent_vg = self._vocab_growth_history[-window:]`.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: IM_F028
SEVERITY: 0.48
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.45
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.should_abort` checks `len(self._active_models) < self.config.k_min` but `k_min` defaults to 1. This means abort only triggers when there are ZERO active models. The docstring says "If only PM survives, framework degrades to single-model mode" — but with `k_min=1`, a single surviving PM is NOT an abort condition. The PM-not-active check above handles PM loss, but the `k_min` check is effectively dead code at the default value. If a non-PM model is the sole survivor (PM was excluded but not via the PM-specific ABORT path — e.g., PM was manually removed from `_active_models`), the system continues with 1 model and no PM, which violates the HARD constraint that PM failure should abort.
PROPOSED_FIX: Either raise `k_min` default to 2 (ensuring at least PM + one other model), or add an explicit check: `if pm_id is not None and pm_id in self._active_models and len(self._active_models) == 1: return False  # single-model degradation, not abort`. Document the intended semantics of `k_min` — is it "minimum total models" or "minimum non-PM models"?
VERIFIED: TRUE
